\section[\texorpdfstring{\fa{اضطراب} (ezterâb)}{اضطراب (ezterâb)}]{\fa{اضطراب} (ezterâb) — anxiety}

\label{lesson:FA-C485-ezterab}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Persian for depressed, then the Persian for sorry.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \fa{اضطراب}}
\textbf{\fa{اضطراب}} (\emph{ezterâb}) — \textquotedblleft{}anxiety\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\fa{قبل} \fa{از} \fa{امتحان} \fa{اضطراب} \fa{دارم}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{qabl az emtehân ezterâb dâram.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
I feel anxious before an exam.
\end{quote}

\emph{ezterâb dâshtan} — to be anxious. Formal; in speech \emph{esteres} is more usual.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{ezterâb} is a loan, usually traced to Arabic \emph{iḍṭirāb}, 'agitation, unrest'. EtymDB has no entry for it.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\fa{استرس} (esteres)}{استرس (esteres)}]{\fa{استرس} (esteres) — stress}

\label{lesson:FA-C485-esteres}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Persian for sorry, then the Persian for anxiety.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \fa{استرس}}
\textbf{\fa{استرس}} (\emph{esteres}) — \textquotedblleft{}stress\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\fa{کار} \fa{زیاد} \fa{به} \fa{او} \fa{استرس} \fa{میدهد}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{kâr-e ziyâd be u esteres midahad.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
A lot of work stresses him out.
\end{quote}

\emph{esteres dâshtan} — to be stressed; \emph{esteres dâdan} — to cause stress. Persian breaks up the \emph{st-} cluster with vowels.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{esteres} is a modern loan, usually traced to English \emph{stress}, with vowels added to fit Persian syllables. EtymDB has no entry for it.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\fa{دلشوره} (delshure)}{دلشوره (delshure)}]{\fa{دلشوره} (delshure) — a nagging worry; butterflies}

\label{lesson:FA-C485-delshure}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Persian for anxiety, then the Persian for stress.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \fa{دلشوره}}
\textbf{\fa{دلشوره}} (\emph{delshure}) — \textquotedblleft{}a nagging worry; butterflies\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\fa{شب} \fa{قبل} \fa{از} \fa{سفر} \fa{دلشوره} \fa{داشتم}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{shab-e qabl az safar delshure dâshtam.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
The night before the trip I had butterflies.
\end{quote}

\emph{del} 'heart' + \emph{shure} 'stirring'. \emph{delshure dâshtan} — to feel uneasy.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{delshure} is built on \emph{del}, 'heart', which EtymDB traces to Middle Persian (EtymDB), and \emph{shure}, usually linked with \emph{shuridan}, 'to be stirred up': a churning heart.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\fa{کلافه} (kalâfe)}{کلافه (kalâfe)}]{\fa{کلافه} (kalâfe) — exasperated, fed up}

\label{lesson:FA-C485-kalafe}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Persian for stress, then the Persian for a nagging worry.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \fa{کلافه}}
\textbf{\fa{کلافه}} (\emph{kalâfe}) — \textquotedblleft{}exasperated, fed up\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\fa{او} \fa{از} \fa{گرمای} \fa{تابستان} \fa{کلافه} \fa{شده} \fa{است}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{u az garmâ-ye tâbestân kalâfe shode ast.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
She's worn out by the summer heat.
\end{quote}

Colloquial and very common: \emph{kalâfe shodam} — I'm fed up.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{kalâfe} also names a skein of yarn, and a tangled skein is the picture behind the feeling. No source used here gives its history, and its origin is not settled.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\fa{آه} \fa{کشیدن} (âh keshidan)}{آه کشیدن (âh keshidan)}]{\fa{آه} \fa{کشیدن} (âh keshidan) — to sigh}

\label{lesson:FA-C485-ah-keshidan}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Persian for a nagging worry, then the Persian for exasperated.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \fa{آه} \fa{کشیدن}}
\textbf{\fa{آه} \fa{کشیدن}} (\emph{âh keshidan}) — \textquotedblleft{}to sigh\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\fa{او} \fa{به} \fa{پنجره} \fa{نگاه} \fa{کرد} \fa{و} \fa{آه} \fa{کشید}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{u be panjere negâh kard va âh keshid.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
She looked at the window and sighed.
\end{quote}

\emph{âh} 'a sigh' + \emph{keshidan} 'to pull, to draw'; present stem \emph{kesh-}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{âh} is usually explained as imitative, built on the sound of a sigh itself, and \emph{keshidan}, 'to pull, to draw', is inherited Persian: to draw a sigh.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}
